title: A Question About Fasting and a Call to Justice
summary: Two years after the night visions, a delegation from Bethel asks whether they should keep fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for many years in mourning for the temple. God answers with a question of his own: were those fasts ever really for him? He then repeats what the earlier prophets said, do justice, show loyal love and compassion, and do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor, and reminds them that their fathers' refusal to listen brought the exile.
story: With chapter 7 the book leaves the night visions and moves forward about two years. The temple is now well along; it will be finished in a little over two years. The practical question this raises is whether the mourning rituals for the old temple's destruction should continue. The answer in chapters 7 and 8 moves in two directions. Chapter 7 looks back, warning the people not to repeat the history that led to the exile. Chapter 8 looks forward, promising that the fasts will become feasts. Together they form the book's sermon on what true religion looks like, and they close the first half of Zechariah.
historical:
Verse 1 dates the word to the fourth day of the ninth month, Chislev, in Darius's fourth year, around December 518 BC. The temple was completed in the twelfth month of Darius's sixth year, 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).

The fasts recalled the disasters of 587 and 586 BC. The fast of the fifth month mourned the burning of the temple and the city by the Babylonian commander Nebuzaradan (2 Kings 25:8-9; Jeremiah 52:12-13). The fast of the seventh month (verse 5) most likely mourned the assassination of Gedaliah, the governor the Babylonians had appointed over Judah, whose murder scattered the remaining community (2 Kings 25:25-26; Jeremiah 41:1-3). The seventy years of verse 5 is the period since the destruction, roughly from 586 to 518 BC. Bethel, about twelve miles (around 19 kilometers) north of Jerusalem, had been a royal shrine of the northern kingdom and was resettled after the exile (Ezra 2:28; Nehemiah 7:32). The delegates' names, Sharezer and Regem-melech, are Babylonian or Akkadian in form, a sign of the exile's lasting influence; the Hebrew can also be read to mean that a man named Bethel-sharezer sent them.
cultural:
Fasting in Israel meant going without food, usually from dawn to evening, often with sackcloth, ashes, weeping, and prayer. The law commanded only one annual fast, the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29-31), but individuals and the community fasted in times of grief, repentance, or danger. After 586 BC the exiles added commemorative fasts for the national catastrophe, and later Jewish tradition kept them as the fast of the Ninth of Av, the Fast of Gedaliah, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, and the Tenth of Tevet.

The list of the vulnerable in verse 10, the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner, and the poor, is the Old Testament's standard list of people without protection in an ancient society. Widows and orphans had lost the male head of household who would defend them in court and support them; foreigners (resident aliens) had no land and no clan; the poor had no reserves. The law repeatedly commanded care for them (Deuteronomy 10:18-19; 24:17-22), and the prophets measured the nation's faithfulness by how it treated them. The Negev and the foothills (Shephelah) in verse 7 were the dry south and the low hills to the west, regions that had been well populated before the Babylonian invasions and were largely empty in Zechariah's time.
literary: The chapter is built as a question and answer, but God's answer does not directly address the question. Instead of ruling on the fast, he asks a counter-question (verses 5-6) and then preaches a sermon from history (verses 7-14). The sermon echoes the earlier prophets deliberately, as Zechariah did in 1:4-6, and its commands in verses 9-10 are a compact summary of the prophetic message, close to Micah 6:8 and Isaiah 1:17. Verses 11-12 describe refusal with a sequence of bodily images: a stubborn shoulder, stopped ears, a heart of flint. Verse 13 turns the refusal into a principle: as they would not listen when God called, he would not listen when they called. The direct answer about the fasts waits until 8:18-19.

outline.t: The delegation from Bethel asks about fasting
Was it really for Me that you fasted?
Why the exile came: hearts like flint

doctrines.note: The heart of the law, as the prophets summarized it, is justice and mercy toward others, especially the defenseless. God's question about fasting reveals that ritual without that heart misses the point, whatever its sincerity.
The law and the words of the earlier prophets were sent by God's Spirit (verse 12). The chapter treats the prophetic tradition as God's own voice, which is why refusing it was so serious.

The exile was not an accident of politics but the result of a people who refused to listen. God called and they would not hear, so when they called he would not hear. Judgment is the consequence of a long refusal, and the pleasant land became a desolation.

words.note: Tsum, to fast. It means to go without food as an act of grief, humility, or prayer. The delegation asks whether to continue; God asks whether their fasting was ever directed toward him at all, turning a question about the calendar into a question about the heart.

Chesed, loyal love, kindness, or covenant faithfulness. It is the steadfast love that keeps commitments and goes beyond them. The BSB renders it loving devotion in verse 9, where it is set beside justice and compassion as what God wants his people to show one another.

Mishpat, justice or judgment. It covers the fair decision of a court and the right order of a community in which the weak are protected. Verse 9 calls for true justice, justice that does not bend to bribes or power.

Shamir, a hard stone, perhaps flint or diamond; elsewhere the word can mean thorn. Ezekiel 3:9 uses it for something harder than flint. The fathers made their hearts like this stone so that God's word could make no mark on them.

christ: Jesus stood squarely in this prophetic line. He taught that fasting done to be seen by others has its reward already (Matthew 6:16-18), and when asked why his disciples did not fast, he said that the wedding guests cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them (Matthew 9:14-15), a note that anticipates Zechariah 8's promise that fasts would become feasts. He rebuked religious leaders who tithed carefully but neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23), almost the same three things Zechariah names. The New Testament also sees Jesus as the one who fulfilled the law's demand for justice and mercy and who now sends his Spirit to write that law on hearts of flesh rather than stone (2 Corinthians 3:3; Ezekiel 36:26). The link is one of continuity: the prophets' demand and Jesus's teaching are the same demand.

hard.q: Is God rejecting fasting and religious ritual altogether?
hard.a: No, and the chapter should not be read that way. God does not forbid the fasts, and in 8:19 he promises to turn them into feasts rather than abolishing them. The law itself commanded worship, sacrifice, and the Day of Atonement fast. What the prophets consistently attack is ritual cut off from justice and mercy, worship that coexists with oppression (Isaiah 58:3-7; Amos 5:21-24). Interpreters in the Jewish and Christian traditions have read this chapter as a call to integrate outward practice and inward faithfulness rather than to choose between them. Some Protestant readers have stressed the danger of trusting ritual, while Catholic, Orthodox, and Jewish readers have stressed that faithful ritual is itself formed by the prophetic call; both agree that the chapter's target is empty religion, not religion itself.

questions: The people had fasted for seventy years, and God asked whether it had been for him. What habits of your faith might need that question?
The widow, the orphan, the foreigner, and the poor were the most exposed people in Zechariah's world. Who holds those places in your community?
The fathers made their hearts like flint by refusing to listen over time. What practices keep a heart soft toward God's word?
